summary: This RFC defines a package for the Media Control Channel Framework that manages mixers for media conferences and connections. It specifies request elements for controlling mixers, including mixers between conferences or connections, along with responses and notifications. It also provides elements to audit package capabilities and mixers.

plainLanguage.summary: In a group call, a mixer blends everyone's voices together. This defines the messages used to tell a mixer what to blend, and to ask it what it can do.

questions: how to control a conference mixer
what is the mediactrl mixer control package
how does a media server mix a conference
subtitle: XML commands that let an application server tell a media server how to mix audio and video for conferences and bridged calls.

tldr.problem: An application server that runs conferencing services needs a standard way to tell a separate media server to create conference mixers, connect call legs together and report what it is doing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Media Control Channel Framework package named msc-mixer/1.0. It uses XML elements such as createconference, join, unjoin and audit, carried in CONTROL and REPORT messages, with numeric status codes for results.
tldr.outcome: It gives MEDIACTRL a full set of mixer operations, notifications and auditing, and requires that mixers are managed only over the control channel that created them.

today: RFC 6505 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the Media Control Channel Framework in RFC 6230.

sections.title: What the Mixer Package Is For
sections.content:
The Media Control Channel Framework (RFC 6230) lets one machine send commands to another over a reliable channel set up with SIP. It introduces Control Packages, each of which is a specific use of the framework. RFC 6505 defines one for media conference mixers and media connection mixers.

The package has elements to create, modify and delete conference mixers, to join, modify and unjoin media streams between connections and conferences, and to audit capabilities and mixers. It was designed to meet media-mixing requirements in RFC 5167 and provides the major conferencing functions of the older media server languages MSCML (RFC 5022) and MSML (RFC 5707), but over the Control Framework.

Out of scope are personalized video mixes for each participant, floor control protocols, and video overlays and text insertion. These can come from extensions or other packages.
sections.plainLanguage: A remote control for a sound mixing desk. The RFC lists the buttons and the messages each button sends.

sections.title: Roles and Vocabulary
sections.content:
Two roles matter. The Application Server (AS) is a SIP application server that hosts services such as interactive media and conferencing and acts as the control client. The Media Server (MS) processes media streams for it, offering conferencing, interactive media and transcoding. In this package the MS is the Control Server that receives requests, and it also acts as a Control Client when it sends event notifications.

An MS Conference provides the mixing resources for a conference. An MS Connection is the end of one or more RTP sessions on the media server, tied to a single SIP dialog. A media stream is a flow of audio or video between a connection and a conference, between two connections, or between two conferences, and can be bidirectional or unidirectional.
sections.plainLanguage: The application server is the director and the media server is the sound crew that does the mixing. A conference is the big mixing desk, and a connection is one person's microphone and speaker.

sections.title: Package Name and Message Bodies
sections.content:
The package is named msc-mixer/1.0. All messages are XML with a root element <mscmixer> that has a mandatory version attribute fixed at "1.0" and an optional desclang attribute for the language of descriptive text, defaulting to i-default. Only one child element can appear in a message. The media type is application/msc-mixer+xml.

Requests (<createconference>, <modifyconference>, <destroyconference>, <join>, <modifyjoin>, <unjoin> and <audit>) travel in CONTROL messages from the AS to the MS. Responses return in a framework 200 response or in REPORT message bodies, as <response> or <auditresponse>. Notifications go the other way, as <event> in CONTROL messages from the MS, and the AS MUST answer them with a Control Framework 200 response.

The schema allows elements and attributes from other namespaces. An MS that gets foreign content it does not support answers with a 428 response. Where the text and the schema differ, the text takes priority.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is a small labelled envelope with the same outer wrapper. Inside is one request, one answer or one announcement.

sections.title: Conference Mixers and Their Settings
sections.content:
<createconference> makes a new multiparty mixer. It may carry a conferenceid (if omitted, the MS MUST create a unique name), reserved-talkers and reserved-listeners (both defaulting to 0), and optional child elements for <codecs>, <audio-mixing>, <video-layouts>, <video-switch> and <subscribe>. If any setting cannot be honored, the MS MUST NOT create the conference and reports a specific error. <modifyconference> changes these settings later, and <destroyconference> removes the mixer and triggers unjoin and exit notifications.

Audio mixing has a type of nbest (default; the N loudest participants are mixed) or controller (the AS picks contributors through an external floor control protocol). With nbest, the n attribute sets how many, and 0 means everyone who contributes audio.

Video layouts are chosen by the number of participants. Each <video-layout> has a min-participants attribute (default 1), and the active layout is the one with the highest minimum not above the current participant count. An MS MAY support the predefined layouts from the XCON data model (RFC 6501).

Video switching decides which participant appears in which region. <vas/> (voice-activated switching) shows the loudest speaker who provides both audio and video, and a speaker must stay loudest for the interval (default 3 seconds) before the switch. <controller/> lets the AS place streams manually. Regions left over are filled by priority: the lower the number, the higher the priority, with 100 as default.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a conference is like arranging a video wall. You say how many speakers to blend, how to split the screen as more people arrive, and whether the screen follows whoever is talking loudest.

sections.title: Joining Streams Together
sections.content:
<join> creates media streams between two entities named by the mandatory id1 and id2 attributes. Each is a connection or a conference. Streams can be audio or video and bidirectional or unidirectional. A bidirectional stream is treated as two one-way streams that can be controlled independently.

A conference mixer uses an "n-minus mix" so that participants do not hear themselves: each participant's own input is subtracted from the sum. For simpler cases, the RFC RECOMMENDS that a media server be able to automatically mix at least two audio streams by plain summing, for example for a "whisper announcement" or a call-center coaching scenario in which a supervisor can speak to an agent without the customer hearing. When a <join> arrives, the MS MUST either mix the new streams with those already joined, or fail without changing anything.

Child <stream> elements tune each flow. Attributes are media (such as audio or video), an optional SDP label and direction (sendrecv by default, sendonly, recvonly or inactive). Inside can be <volume> (automatic, setgain in dB, or setstate to mute or unmute), <clamp> (removes DTMF tones; by default all of them), <region> and <priority>.

<modifyjoin> reconfigures existing streams. A direction left out of a <modifyjoin> is dropped, so to keep a direction its <stream> must still be listed. <unjoin> removes the named streams, or all streams between the two entities when none are named.
sections.plainLanguage: Joining is plugging a cable between two things, such as a person and the mixing desk. You can also turn the volume up or down on each cable, or unplug it.

sections.title: Notifications and Auditing
sections.content:
The MS announces things with <event>. <active-talkers-notify> lists the current speakers, subscribed to with <active-talkers-sub>, whose interval (default 3 seconds) is the minimum time between events, and 0 suppresses further notifications. <unjoin-notify> says a join ended, with status 0 (an unjoin request), 1 (execution error) or 2 (a connection or conference ended). <conferenceexit> MUST be sent whenever a successfully created conference exits, with status 0 (destroy request), 1 (execution error) or 2 (maximum duration exceeded). After it, the conference identifier can be reused.

<audit> lets the AS discover what the MS can do and what mixers exist. The attributes capabilities and mixers both default to true, and conferenceid narrows the report to one conference. The <auditresponse> holds <capabilities> (the available codecs) and <mixers> (<conferenceaudit> and <joinaudit> entries). Auditing is useful before creating mixers and when one AS takes over from another that failed.

Codecs are described with <codec>, which has a name (the media type) and a <subtype>, plus optional <params>.
sections.plainLanguage: The mixer can tap the director on the shoulder to say who is talking or that the party is over. The director can also ask what the mixer can do and what is running right now.

sections.title: Response Status Codes
sections.content:
Every request gets a <response> with a numeric status. These package codes are separate from the Control Framework's own error codes, which cover things like invalid XML. A failed request is all or nothing: the MS MUST make sure no part of the requested operation is carried out and answer with a 4xx code.

Failures fall into three groups: a syntax error (400), an error executing the request (405 to 419) and a capability the MS lacks (420 to 435). The MS SHOULD use the most specific code. An AS that sees an unknown code treats it as the x00 code for its class, so an unrecognized 499 is handled like 400. It SHOULD NOT retry the same request unchanged, although the same request sent to a different MS might succeed.
sections.plainLanguage: Answers come with numbers, like a teacher's marks. If the mixer cannot do all of what you asked, it does none of it and tells you which kind of problem it hit.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST handle the security issues of XML in RFC 3023 and the channel security rules in RFC 6230, which cover transport protection, channel policy and the SIP and RTP sessions with the MS. The RFC lists two attacks. In denial of service, an attacker could inject a message such as <destroyconference> with a guessed or audited conference identifier, or impersonate the MS and send error responses. In resource exhaustion, an attacker could inject many <createconference> requests until the MS runs out of mixers.

The package adds a channel-scoping policy. The MS MUST send responses and notifications only on the control channel that carried the request or created the mixer, and MUST only audit mixers created on the same channel. It SHOULD reject audit or manipulation requests from a different channel with a Control Framework 403 response.

The RFC admits valid reasons to allow exceptions, such as an administrator who needs a separate channel to audit mixers, or a replacement AS that takes over a failed one by reusing the same channel identifier. Implementations must weigh the implications and reject such requests unless the reasons really apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the person who made a mixer may boss it around, so a stranger cannot shut off a conference or fill the desk with fake ones.
